svg.aria-label: Diagram: Conditional Access on Microsoft Entra, showing the two-phase evaluation with its fixed grant control prompt order, the default-allow behaviour in which an access token is issued when no policy condition triggers a control, the propagation delays before a policy or group change takes effect, and the boundaries of what Conditional Access is not
svg.title: Conditional Access evaluates at token issuance, and everything surprising follows from that
svg.text: Conditional Access decides at token issuance. Everything surprising follows from that.
It is a policy engine, not a gate. It runs after the password has already been accepted, and only when a token is being minted.
Two phases, and a prompt order that is fixed rather than configurable
PHASE 1
Collect session details — network location, device identity. Report-only policies run here too.
PHASE 2
Block stops here. “If there’s a policy that is configured with the block grant control,
enforcement stops here and the user is blocked.”
Otherwise the unmet grant controls are prompted, always in this order:
1 MFA → 2 compliant device → 3 hybrid joined → 4 approved client app → 5 app protection policy
→ 6 password change → 7 terms of use → 8 custom controls, then session controls
The default is allow. A policy that requires MFA for a group does not keep anyone else out.
“Access tokens are issued by default if a Conditional Access policy condition doesn’t trigger an access control.”
POLICY 1 — what most people write
Finance group → Payroll app → require MFA
User A, in Finance: prompted for MFA.
User B, not in Finance: walks in. No MFA.
POLICY 2 — the one that actually restricts
All users, except Finance → Payroll → block
Restriction needs its own explicit policy.
A requirement is not a restriction.
When a change actually takes effect — none of these is immediate
You add a user to a targeted group
not until their next token — “the policy doesn’t apply retroactively”
You edit a policy, or change a group
“could take up to one day” to reach Exchange and SharePoint
A critical event fires under CAE
near real time, but “latency of up to 15 minutes might be observed”
A user moves outside an allowed IP range
“IP locations policy enforcement is instant” — the one exception
You re-enable an account you disabled
15 min for SharePoint and Teams; 35–40 min for Exchange Online
You need it now
revoke the refresh tokens. That is the only immediate lever.
What it is not
“Conditional Access policies are enforced after
first-factor authentication is completed.” It is not a
“frontline defense for scenarios like denial-of-service”.
It does not stop service principals: “Calls made by
service principals aren’t blocked by Conditional Access
policies scoped to users.”
And device platform comes from “unverified sources”.
Limits worth knowing before you design
240 policies per tenant, hard, counting every policy
“in any state, including report-only mode, on, or off”.
New policies apply to every client app type by default,
configured or not. Multiple grant controls default to all.
CAE does not cover guest accounts at all.
Deleted policies are recoverable for 30 days.
Sources: Conditional Access overview, Build Conditional Access policies, Plan your deployment, and Continuous access evaluation, on Microsoft Learn.
